column1: ∀ and ∃ on a finite domain, in Python
column2: ∀x∈D. P(x) is all(P(x) for x in D); ∃x∈D. P(x) is any(P(x) for x in D).

column1: The quantifier game: who picks at ∀, who picks at ∃, and when is the statement true?
column2: Opponent picks at ∀, you pick at ∃, left to right, seeing earlier picks. True iff you can always win.

column1: ∀x ∃y. x + y = 4 vs ∃y ∀x. x + y = 4 over D = {0..4}
column2: First true (y = 4 − x can depend on x). Second false (one y must work for every x).

column1: On a grid of P(x, y) (rows x, columns y), what do ∀x ∃y and ∃y ∀x mean?
column2: ∀x ∃y: every row has a dot. ∃y ∀x: some column is full.
∃y∀x ⇒ ∀x∃y (a full column gives every row a dot). The reverse fails: the diagonal x = y is a counter-model (MCS §3.6.6, pp. 67–68).

column1: Hashing: '∀ key sets S ∃ h with no collisions' vs '∃ h ∀ S no collisions' (more keys than slots)
column2: First true; second false by pigeonhole. That's hash flooding: with h fixed, an attacker picks colliding keys. Hence randomised hash seeds.
NOT ∀x. P(x) ≡ ∃x. NOT P(x); NOT ∃x. P(x) ≡ ∀x. NOT P(x) (MCS §3.6.5, p. 66). In Python: not all(...) == any(not ...).
∃x ∀y. y ≤ x. Move the NOT right, flipping each quantifier it passes.

column1: How do you write 'for all' in SQL?
column2: As NOT EXISTS … NOT EXISTS: 'no course the student hasn't taken' = 'took every course'.

column1: What's wrong with: negation of 'every request is fast' is 'every request is slow'?
column2: The quantifier must flip: the negation is 'some request is slow'. One counterexample is enough.

column1: How do you show a quantified formula is NOT valid?
column2: Give a counter-model: a domain and an interpretation that make it false (MCS §3.6.6, p. 68).

column1: Why avoid the word 'any' in specs and proofs?
column2: It can mean ∀ or ∃: 'if you can solve any problem, you get an A' (MCS §3.6.1, p. 64). Say 'every' or 'some'.
